bluf.text: Poland is building the largest land army in the EU, funded at a record ~4.8% of GDP, postured for homeland and forward defence of NATO's eastern flank and absorbing Western and South Korean kit at exceptional speed.

key_facts.text: Armed forces have grown to more than 220,000 personnel, with a planned expansion toward ~500,000 (active + reserves) by the late 2030s.
2026 defence budget is a record ~200 billion złoty (~$53–55B), ~4.8% of GDP — approaching the NATO 5% goal.
Tank fleet heading toward ~1,100 (250 M1A2 SEPv3 Abrams, 116 M1A1, ~180+ K2 with more to follow) once deals complete by 2030.
Doctrine centres on territorial and forward defence of 'every inch', anchored on NATO Article 5 and US presence.

snapshot.so_what_saf: Poland is the clearest live laboratory for high-intensity land war, counter-UAS and mass mobilisation in Europe — a cold-start, learn-from partner where the value is method, not materiel.

summary.text: Land Forces built around four standing armoured/mechanised divisions plus two divisions forming, with airborne and air-cavalry brigades.

active_personnel.text: ~220,000+ active personnel (all services); land forces the bulk.

note.text: Reactivated Jan 2023; to be the largest Polish formation, Polish + South Korean equipment, FOC ~end of decade.

trend.note: NATO value comes from the summary table of the March 2023 edition (2014 vs 2022 columns). SIPRI/WDI gives 1.91. The current-USD figure is not verified.
SIPRI via World Bank WDI. Notes from Poland reports NATO data showing about 2.2% 'a decade ago'.

2.42 was an estimate in NATO's March 2023 edition, and later editions may revise it. The SIPRI/WDI snapshot gives 2.20; footnotes say this series excludes some defence spending outside the MoD budget.

The NATO value is from the June 2024 edition. The SIPRI % comes from the latest World Bank vintage via Trading Economics; an older UNdata snapshot shows 3.27, so SIPRI vintages differ. USD is SIPRI (26,342.8m) via Trading Economics.

3.76 is the revised NATO figure in the 2025 edition and the SG Annual Report. NATO's June 2024 estimate had been 4.12. SIPRI reports $38.0bn and 4.2% of GDP. NATO's June 2024 USD estimate was about $35bn.

4.48 is NATO's August 2025 estimate, the highest in NATO. The NATO SG Annual Report of March 2026 gives 4.3%. SIPRI gives $46.8bn and 4.5% of GDP, the highest military burden in NATO. NATO's USD estimate is $44.3bn.
4.68 is NATO's 2026 estimate (constant 2021 prices) as reported by ICDS; NATO's 2014-2026 edition itself was not retrieved. The national 2026 budget plans 4.8% of GDP, about $55bn.

notes.text: Fiscal strain is real — public-finance deficit could be among the EU's largest; watch the enacted budget law vs the draft.

posture.text: Homeland + forward defence along the eastern border — 'defend every inch', explicitly rejecting trading space for time; deterrence rests on NATO Article 5 and US presence.

doctrine.text: Shift since 2014 away from post-Cold-War expeditionary posture back to territorial defence.
Analysts note doctrine still catching up to the new force structure; Poland well placed to adapt Ukrainian combat lessons (hosts NATO-Ukraine JATEC).

programmes.text: Eastern Shield (Tarcza Wschód): ~€2B fortification/barrier belt along the Belarus/Kaliningrad border — anti-tank ditches, bunkers, sensors and EW to slow the enemy and keep own forces moving.

current.text: Abrams: 250 M1A2 SEPv3 (deliveries through 2026) plus 116 M1A1.
K2 Black Panther: ~180 delivered/ordered under Wilk, with a second batch — toward ~1,100 total tanks by 2030.
HIMARS/Homar: framework for ~486 launcher kits (figures vary; treat large totals as ceilings).
FA-50 light combat aircraft: 48 ordered (GF delivered 2023; PL variant 2025–2028).
AH-64E Apache attack helicopters and 32 F-35A on order.

emerging.text: Counter-UAS: 18 SAN very-short-range batteries from Kongsberg (~$1.6B), radar + layered effectors, built around Ukraine lessons.
Three-track air defence: Wisła (medium), Narew (short), SAN (very-short) — layered, with low-cost interceptors.
EW and GNSS-jamming resistance embedded in the Eastern Shield belt; nationwide counter-drone expansion intended.
Fast-growing domestic defence industry — procurement from Polish firms ~quadrupled since 2022 to ~$8.2B/yr.

bio.text: Physician (Jagiellonian University medicine graduate, doctorate in medical sciences 2010) and leader of the Polish People's Party (PSL) since 2015. Minister of Labour and Social Policy 2011–2015; elected by the Sejm on 12 Dec 2023 and appointed Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence on 13 Dec 2023. In Oct 2026 he used the Warsaw Security Forum to announce a 'small strategic review' of urgent procurement.

positions.text: Poland will run a 'small strategic review' to buy the most urgently needed equipment, weighing delivery times and industrial capacity; key areas are low-cost long-range precision strike, drone and counter-drone systems, and AI — and he urged allies to do the same.
Europe's defence industry should move to a 'war-mode' production footing, and US firms should set up production in Europe (e.g. relocating Patriot production).
Backs a half-million-strong armed force as a long-term goal and framed 2026 as the year of building reserves (MoND annual review, Feb 2026).
Launched Operation SZPEJ (Jan 2024) to modernise soldiers' individual kit and weapons.

interests.text: Medicine: a physician who returned to practise as a volunteer at a Kraków hospital for some weeks during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021 (press reports).
Grassroots/rural sport: chaired the Main Council of the National Association of Rural Sports Clubs (LZS) 2012–2021 (official bio).

hooks.text: Start from his own WSF 2026 priority list — counter-drone, AI and affordable long-range precision strike. These overlap with SAF/DIS priorities (C-UAS, AI-enabled sense-making), so offer expert-level exchanges rather than procurement talk.

A doctor-turned-minister who volunteered in a COVID-19 hospital in 2021. Military medicine and whole-of-government crisis response are natural rapport topics where Singapore has its own pandemic experience to share.

Precedent exists for senior SG–PL contact (SM Teo Chee Hean in Warsaw, May 2023), and Poland sent a deputy defence minister to Shangri-La Dialogue 2025. A realistic first ask is to invite him personally to SLD or seek a bilateral on the margins of the Warsaw Security Forum.

bio.text: Career special-forces officer (Iraq 2003) who commanded the Special Forces Group in Lubliniec from 2012 and in 2016 became the first commander of the Territorial Defence Forces (WOT). He was General Commander of the Armed Forces from Feb 2023, was entrusted with the duties of Chief of the General Staff on 10 Oct 2023 and was promoted to four-star general on 9 Nov 2023. President Nawrocki has reappointed him for a further three-year term from 10 Oct 2026.

education.text: Graduate of the Higher Officer School of Signal Forces (Military Academy of the Signal Corps), Zegrze.
Master's degree in electronics and telecommunications, Military University of Technology (WAT), Warsaw. Sources disagree on the year (2001 or 2003).
Postgraduate studies in defence policy, War Studies Academy (Akademia Sztuki Wojennej), Warsaw. He also completed a Higher Specialist Course (Wyższy Kurs Specjalistyczny).
No foreign staff or war college course appears in the NATO, EEAS or MoND biographies checked.

positions.text: Polish and allied intelligence indicate that Russia is organising and developing the capacity for conventional war with NATO, and he expects this to accelerate once Russia reaches 'acceptable' political and military aims in Ukraine.
2026 is the 'year of reserves', the start of a multi-year rebuild. A new reserve model aims for a force of up to ~500,000, and 2026 pilots will test the reserve path of the wGotowości programme.
Poland is in a 'pre-war' phase of Russian hybrid aggression (sabotage, cyber), and the outcome depends on whether Poland and its allies invest enough in deterrence.
The main task is to deter Russia from attacking. The 2025–2039 Armed Forces Development Programme centres on high-readiness forces of ~500,000 and long-range strike.

interests.text: Lists his interests as the history of unconventional warfare, project management and photography (official NATO biography).

hooks.text: He has declared 2026 Poland's 'year of reserves' and is piloting a reserve model of up to ~500k. SAF's long experience of managing NS/NSmen reservists is a credible offer, and reserve mobilisation and readiness is a high-value CDF-to-CGS conversation (SAF counterpart: CDF VADM Aaron Beng).

As founding commander of WOT (2016–2023) he built a part-time citizen-soldier force from scratch. That is the closest Polish parallel to Singapore's NS and Total Defence model, so ask him for lessons on recruiting, retention and community roles.

Rapport openers: a commando career (Iraq 2003, JWK command) and his stated interests in the history of unconventional warfare and in photography. These suit SOF-to-SOF exchanges and informal conversation.

leadership.appointment: General Commander of the Branches of the Armed Forces (Dowódca Generalny Rodzajów Sił Zbrojnych)

bio.text: Born in 1966 in Bartoszyce, he was promoted to generał broni (three-star) on 14 Aug 2023. Minister Błaszczak designated him acting General Commander in Oct 2023, and President Duda formally appointed him on 3 May 2024. The General Command is the single command responsible for the Land Forces, Air Force, Navy and Special Forces. In June 2026 he received the U.S. Legion of Merit (Commander) during a visit to the United States.

positions.text: Pushes brigade-level digitisation: during his April 2026 visit to the 20th Mechanised Brigade he showcased progress on the BMS Legion battlefield-management system.
Has publicly discussed a possible Stryker acquisition as an 'armoured leap' for the Polish Army. This is known from the interview headline only; the content was not verified.

Strong US Army ties (Legion of Merit, June 2026; Stryker discussion) make him a useful view on interoperability with US-equipped partners.
His command supports the 'Bezpieczne Podlasie' border operation against hybrid pressure from Belarus, which offers practical grey-zone and hybrid lessons for the SAF.

President Duda handed him his appointment as WOT commander on 3 May 2024, making him the formation's third commander. He holds a doctorate in security sciences and is now reported as generał dywizji (two-star).

positions.text: WOT is expanding its Border Defence Component, fielding Grot A3 rifles as complete weapon systems and widening the use of light drones.
WOT brigades are being professionalised by about 17–18%, and the current stage of change runs to the end of 2026.
2026 is a year of intensive training closely tailored to the brigades' real needs.

hooks.text: WOT is a part-time, volunteer citizen-soldier force that is now being partly professionalised (~17–18%). It is the most direct Polish comparator for SAF NSmen readiness, training-time budgeting and community/total-defence roles.
Light drones at small-unit level and a dedicated Border Defence Component make for practical small-unit drone and C-UAS exchanges.

bio.text: President Nawrocki appointed Grodecki head of the BBN, the President's national-security office, on 8 May 2026. He succeeded Sławomir Cenckiewicz, who resigned in late April 2026. He was deputy interior minister (2020–2023), responsible for migration and border policy, and before the BBN post advised the management board of RADMOR (WB Group), a Gdynia military-communications maker. Press has noted that his name appears in a Supreme Audit Office (NIK) report on visa procedures.

His border/migration portfolio and defence-industry background (RADMOR/WB Group) suit conversations on hybrid border pressure and defence-industrial cooperation. Be mindful of Palace–government splits on defence financing (e.g. SAFE).

scholarship.title: Polish Armed Forces Modernization
scholarship.author: Marcinek & Boston
scholarship.takeaway: Force structure has outrun doctrine; Poland positioned to adapt Ukrainian lessons via JATEC.

scholarship.title: OSW Commentary No. 694 — Ukraine's drone imports
scholarship.takeaway: Drones' front-line weight keeps rising; Poland a significant drone exporter to Ukraine.

scholarship.title: Countering Drones: Five Lessons from Ukraine for NATO's Northeastern Flank
scholarship.takeaway: Sensors, EW, data-sharing, layered protection, low-cost interceptors — cost-per-kill matters.

scholarship.title: Si vis pacem, para bellum: Transformation of the Polish Armed Forces in Response to Emerging Threats
scholarship.author: Rafal Lipka; Sebastian Czub (eds. Tomasz Smura, Slawomir Florek)
scholarship.takeaway: Wargame-based (RAND-supported): Poland is not yet ready for full-scale war, and a 5-10 year horizon of sustained modernisation, transformation and industrial investment is required.

scholarship.title: Weaken, divide and deter: the aims of Russia's provocation against Poland
scholarship.author: OSW (byline not captured)
scholarship.takeaway: The 9-10 Sep 2025 drone incursion was a deliberate probe meant to erode Polish trust in government, military and allies and to show NATO cannot protect members. It triggered NATO's Eastern Sentry.

scholarship.title: NATO Nuclear Adaptation
scholarship.author: Artur Kacprzyk
scholarship.takeaway: Sets out options for adapting NATO's nuclear posture, including Polish participation via nuclear certification of F-35As. This is background for Warsaw's recurring nuclear-sharing ask.

scholarship.title: Poland's navy steps up a weight class
scholarship.author: IISS (byline not captured)
scholarship.takeaway: Naval expansion is ambitious, but with just over 6,000 naval personnel Poland's ability to crew it is in question.

scholarship.title: Defense Budgets in an Uncertain Security Environment (Chapter 13)
scholarship.author: CSIS (byline not captured)
scholarship.takeaway: Estimates Poland at about 4.5% of GDP on defence in 2025, highest in NATO, funded partly through the off-budget Armed Forces Support Fund's bond issuance.

scholarship.title: Does Russian Deterrence Begin in Poland?
scholarship.author: Alexander Lanoszka; Michael Hunzeker
scholarship.takeaway: Revisits, seven years on, the authors' case for a permanent and survivable US presence in Poland as the anchor of deterring Russia.

scholarship.title: Poland's mass-army turn is reshaping NATO's eastern flank
scholarship.author: ASPI The Strategist (byline not captured)
scholarship.takeaway: Poland's expansion to 2039 for sustained high-intensity war breaks with Europe's small expeditionary-force model. It strains an ageing population and public finances and may reset expectations for other allies. Written from an Indo-Pacific vantage, so useful for SAF framing.

scholarship.title: Wojsko Polskie - nowe jednostki, wieksza liczebnosc
scholarship.author: Ministry of National Defence
scholarship.takeaway: Official claim: more than 210,000 soldiers under arms in mid-2025, with new units and a long-term 300,000-strong army goal. Confidence: claimed.

scholarship.author: Warsaw Enterprise Institute (byline not captured)
scholarship.takeaway: Critique of the voluntary civilian training programme: short courses risk an illusion of preparedness rather than real reserve capability, and pull professional instructors away from core training.

sg_ties.text: Poland and Singapore established diplomatic relations. Poland's ambassador has been resident in Singapore since 2004 (embassy at Wisma Atria, Orchard Road).

Singapore has no resident embassy in Poland. A non-resident Singapore ambassador covers Poland, and an honorary consulate-general in Warsaw has operated since 2019. Poland's embassy reports that the non-resident ambassador visits about twice a year.

PMs Lee Hsien Loong and Donald Tusk witnessed the signing of a revised Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement during Tusk's official visit to Singapore. It replaced the 1993 DTA, entered into force on 2014-02-06 and has been modified by the MLI since 2019-04-01. This is economic, not defence.

The EU framework covers Poland as an EU member. The EU–Singapore Digital Trade Agreement entered into force on 2026-02-01 and adds to the EU–Singapore FTA, in force since 2019. Singapore's MFA calls the EUSFTA the cornerstone of bilateral economic ties.

Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security Teo Chee Hean made a working visit to Warsaw on 25–26 May 2023. He met FM Zbigniew Rau and 'other senior Polish officials in charge of national security, defence, and information security'. Topics included trade and investment and the Russia–Ukraine war. This is the closest thing found to a security-level Singapore visit to Poland.

FM Radosław Sikorski made an official visit to Singapore on 2–3 September 2024, marking 55 years of diplomatic relations. He met PM Lawrence Wong, SM Teo Chee Hean and FM Vivian Balakrishnan. The focus was trade, investment, food security and the rules-based order. No defence deliverable was reported.

Deputy Minister of National Defence Paweł Zalewski led Poland's presence at the 22nd IISS Shangri-La Dialogue, together with MFA Undersecretary Robert Kupiecki. Polish defence press reports that his sideline bilateral meetings included defence-ministry representatives from Singapore. No Singapore-side readout was found.

President Andrzej Duda made a State Visit on 11–13 June 2025, the first by a Polish president in over 20 years. He held talks with President Tharman and PM Wong. The Polish account says talks covered advanced technologies 'including digital transformation, defence innovation and green energy'. Duda also met PSA International and ST Engineering to explore maritime logistics, aerospace, cybersecurity and dual-use technology cooperation. No defence agreement was reported signed.

Polish defence press reported Duda's meeting with ST Engineering during the visit. It described ST Engineering as one potential technology supplier for Poland's New Wheeled Armoured Transporter programme, with the Terrex family as a candidate base vehicle. No decision or contract was found.

This is the only concrete Singapore–Poland defence-industrial link found. Niewiadów Polska Grupa Militarna (NPGM) reports a 30-year licence from ST Engineering Advanced Material Engineering to produce 40 mm grenades (40x53 HV, 40x46 LV) for Poland and the EU. It grew out of an MoU disclosed in a September 2025 filing. ST Engineering has not announced it, and the details come from the Polish partner, partly through sponsored content.

Deputy MND Paweł Zalewski was listed as a speaker at the 23rd IISS Shangri-La Dialogue (29–31 May 2026), in a defence-industrial resilience session. This makes two consecutive years of Polish deputy-minister attendance at SLD.

No evidence was found of a Polish national pavilion or official Polish delegation at Singapore Airshow 2026 (3–8 Feb). Poland is absent from the organiser's pre-show list of expected country pavilions.

Overall assessment: Singapore–Poland defence ties are thin. No bilateral defence cooperation agreement, staff talks, exercise or MINDEF news release on Poland was found. Contact is limited to Shangri-La Dialogue sidelines, foreign-ministry and head-of-state visits that mention 'defence innovation', and company-level industrial links (ST Engineering). Engagement would start from close to zero.

venues.name: War Studies University (Akademia Sztuki Wojennej, ASzWoj), Warsaw
venues.note: The highest-level academy of the Polish Armed Forces. It lists English-taught programmes, including Global Affairs and Diplomacy and Military Diplomacy, and runs a joint diploma with the University of Buckingham. An undated Defence24 count put foreign students at 29, mostly civilians across Poland's academies. No source confirms foreign officers in its senior staff or operational courses.

venues.name: Polish Naval Academy (Akademia Marynarki Wojennej), Gdynia
venues.note: Runs English-language course programmes for foreign exchange students under Erasmus. Defence24 reported it had the most foreign students of any Polish military academy (58), though the count is undated. No stated foreign-officer course.

venues.name: Military University of Technology (Wojskowa Akademia Techniczna, WAT), Warsaw
venues.note: Technical military university with Erasmus+ exchange. Defence24 counted 35 foreign students (undated). The Cyberspace Defence Forces were launched there in February 2022. A possible entry point for defence-technology academic links.

venues.name: NATO Joint Force Training Centre (JFTC), Bydgoszcz
venues.note: NATO Command Structure training centre. Its fact sheet says it works on integrating 'national training and command organisations, regional security organisations and partners'. It has a partnership with Georgia's NATO-Georgian JTEC. 'Partners' here means formal NATO partnership countries. As an assessment to verify, Singapore is not one, so access would need NATO approval.

venues.name: NATO–Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC), Bydgoszcz
venues.note: Opened on 2025-02-17 under HQ SACT. It is the first joint NATO–Ukraine body in the NATO Command Structure and is focused on analysing lessons from the war in Ukraine. It is restricted to NATO and Ukraine. Its value to the SAF is any lessons it publishes, not access.

venues.name: NATO Military Police Centre of Excellence (MP COE), Bydgoszcz
venues.note: Poland is the framework nation. It describes itself as training 'leaders and specialists from NATO member and partner countries'. Its 2026 calendar includes junior officer and senior/junior NCO courses and an annual lessons-learned conference (7–11 Dec 2026). Singapore's eligibility as a non-partner is unverified.

venues.name: NATO Counter Intelligence Centre of Excellence (CI COE), Kraków
venues.note: Established in 2015 with Poland and Slovakia as framework nations, plus sponsoring nations (the US joined in 2019). It is the SACT Department Head for counter-intelligence education and training. No partner-access statement was found, and the subject is sensitive, so it is a low priority for a non-NATO partner.

venues.name: HQ Multinational Corps Northeast (MNC NE), Szczecin
venues.note: NATO Force Structure corps HQ focused on deterring attack on NATO's north-eastern territory. It took part in ANAKONDA-23. No partner-access statement was found. A possible venue for a DV or briefing visit, not training.

venues.name: Exercise DRAGON-24
venues.note: Polish-led national exercise within NATO's STEADFAST DEFENDER-24, held in March 2024 (media day 4 March, ran to 14 March). Over 20,000 troops took part, including about 15,000 Polish, with 3,500 pieces of equipment from 9 Allied nations. It featured a Vistula river crossing. No partner-observer programme was stated.

venues.name: Exercise ANAKONDA (series; ANAKONDA-23 most recent confirmed)
venues.note: The Polish Operational Command's main joint-defence exercise, reported as triennial. ANAKONDA-23 (Apr–May 2023) had about 12,000 Polish personnel plus Allied units and the eFP Battlegroup Poland. An ANAKONDA-26 could not be confirmed. It predates the 2024–26 window and is included because it is Poland's flagship series.

venues.name: Exercise IRON DEFENDER-25 (federation of exercises)
venues.note: Poland's largest exercise of 2025, from September 2025. About 30,000 Polish and Allied troops and 600 pieces of equipment took part, with the 18th Mechanised Division as main force in IRON GATE-25. It ran in parallel with Russia–Belarus ZAPAD-2025. No partner-observer statement was found.

venues.name: Exercise CZARNY OBROŃCA-26 (Black Defender-26)
venues.note: A General Command–run federation of exercises (14–24 Sep 2026) on land, at sea and in the air across north-western Poland and the Baltic. Reported at about 11,000 troops, with the 11th Armoured Cavalry Division as main unit. Defence24 reports that the ROK Army Chief of Staff, Gen. Kim Gyu-ha, observed parts of it during a 13–15 Sep visit. That is a non-NATO precedent, but it came with a deep ROK–Poland arms relationship. This is the best evidence that a senior partner observer is possible.

venues.name: MSPO – International Defence Industry Exhibition, Kielce
venues.note: Poland's main defence exhibition, held annually in September. The 34th edition ran 8–11 Sep 2026 with over 1,000 exhibitors from about 40 countries (pre-show figure). Canada was lead nation and PGZ strategic partner. Open to foreign delegations and exhibitors, so it is the natural DTCO/DSTA venue.

venues.name: Warsaw Security Forum
venues.note: Annual Track 1.5 security conference in October. The 2026 edition is 12–13 Oct with more than 2,500 expected participants from 90 countries; Norway is partner nation. A low-cost way to build a network with Polish MoD and General Staff leadership.

venues.name: Defence24 Days, Warsaw
venues.note: Billed as the largest defence conference in Central and Eastern Europe. The 8th edition was held on 6–7 May 2026 at PGE Narodowy, and foreign governments promote it as a trade event. Useful for tracking Polish procurement and the drone/C-UAS debate.

saf_units.name: Defence Policy Group (DPG)
saf_units.role: Handles MINDEF's relations with its foreign counterparts, strategic communications, National Education, Total Defence, strategic planning and futures analysis, and inter-ministry coordination on emerging security threats.

saf_units.name: Defence Policy Office (DPO)
saf_units.role: Develops strategy and directs efforts to strengthen bilateral defence relations with partner countries, build an open and inclusive regional security architecture, and contribute to international security.

saf_units.name: SAFTI Military Institute (SAFTI MI)
saf_units.role: Tri-service, tri-level institute of the SAF and home of the SAF Officer Corps. It includes the Goh Keng Swee Command and Staff College, SAF Advanced Schools, Officer Cadet School and Specialist and Warrant Officer Institute.

saf_units.name: Goh Keng Swee Command and Staff College (GKS CSC)
saf_units.role: Prepares officers for senior command and staff appointments. It is the highest level of formal military education in Singapore for Regular, NS and International Officers, and graduated 23 international officers from 12 countries in 2025. It hosts a Distinguished Leaders Dialogue, which Lithuania's CHOD addressed in 2026.

saf_units.name: HQ Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC), Singapore Army
saf_units.role: Army formation overseeing training integrity and Army-wide standardisation of tactics, techniques and procedures. It has signed a training and doctrine MoA with the US Army Combined Arms Center.

saf_units.name: Combat Service Support Command (CSSCOM), Singapore Army
saf_units.role: Formed in 2006 to bring together all functional combat service support expertise to support Army units across the full range of operations.

saf_units.name: Digital and Intelligence Service (DIS)
saf_units.role: The SAF's fourth service, inaugurated in October 2022. It raises, trains and sustains digital forces and capabilities, with a mission to 'defend and dominate in the digital domain' across intelligence, C4 and cyber.

saf_units.name: SAF C4 & Digitalisation Command
saf_units.role: DIS command for SAF C4 and digitalisation. It was renamed from SAF C4 Command in March 2025, with the Digital Ops-Tech Centre placed under it.

saf_units.name: Defence Cyber Command
saf_units.role: DIS command inaugurated in March 2025 from the Cybersecurity Task Force and Defence Cyber Organisation. It defends MINDEF/SAF against cyber threats and partners Whole-of-Government to support national cyber defence.

saf_units.name: Air Defence and Operations Command (ADOC), RSAF
saf_units.role: Protects the integrity of Singapore's territorial airspace and provides air defence for homeland security. It raises, trains and sustains the RSAF's Ground Based Air Defence and Command & Control forces.

saf_units.name: RSAF UAS Warfare and Tactics Centre
saf_units.short: RSAF UAS Warfare and Tactics Centre
saf_units.role: Leads efforts to develop counter-UAS strategies and integrate them with the broader SAF. Announced in 2025.

saf_units.name: SAF Counter-UAS Development and Operations Group
saf_units.short: SAF Counter-UAS Development and Operations Group
saf_units.role: Announced by the Minister for Defence on 2025-03-03, to be formed with other government agencies. It targets the small-drone threat, adding sensors, jammers and weapons to existing air defence. Its stand-up date is not confirmed in sources found.

saf_units.name: Drone Accelerator for Rapid Equipping (DARE), Singapore Army
saf_units.role: Army initiative announced in 2025 to quickly equip the force with UAS and scale up UAV and unmanned ground vehicle operations. Exact status is not confirmed.

saf_units.name: Central Manpower Base (CMPB)
saf_units.role: Handles National Service registration, pre-enlistment medical examination and deferment applications under the Enlistment Act.

saf_units.name: Nexus
saf_units.role: The lead agency in MINDEF/SAF that drives National Education and Total Defence. Total Defence has six pillars: military, civil, economic, social, digital and psychological.

saf_units.name: Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA)
saf_units.role: MINDEF statutory board, formed in 2000, that performs acquisitions management, systems management and systems development for MINDEF and the SAF across the system life cycle.

saf_units.name: DSO National Laboratories
saf_units.role: Defence R&D organisation in MINDEF's Defence Technology Community, described as Singapore's largest defence R&D organisation. It researches emerging technologies and develops defence systems for the SAF.

saf_units.name: Future Systems and Technology Directorate (FSTD)

precedents.text: Since 1998 the RSAF has stationed its Advanced Jet Training Detachment (150 Squadron, M-346) at Cazaux Air Base. It has more than 250 RSAF instructors, trainees, engineers, support staff and their families, and trains aircrew for the F-15SG and F-16 beyond Singapore's airspace limits. A Minister of State visited in June 2025 for the Singapore–France 60th anniversary. This is a permanent training detachment, the highest form of SAF–European engagement.

Exercise PANZER STRIKE is an annual armour live-firing exercise in Germany, held since 2009 and at Oberlausitz Military Training Area since 2016. Its 17th edition (28 Feb–19 Mar 2026) had about 80 personnel from 48 SAR with Leopard 2SG and Hunter AFVs alongside Panzergrenadierbataillon 391.

Singapore and Germany signed a Defence Cooperation Agreement in 2005 and an enhanced DCA in 2018. The eDCA anchors bilateral training and policy cooperation, and is a model for a framework agreement with a European partner.

The 2018 Defence Cooperation MoU with the UK underpins defence ties under the UK–Singapore Strategic Partnership. The Minister for Defence made a working visit in October 2024 and met Defence Secretary John Healey. A cooperative defence research MoU was renewed in 2018.

Singapore and Sweden signed an amendment to their Defence Technology MoU on 2024-11-15 during the Swedish King's state visit. It adds defence innovation, covering dual-use collaboration with start-ups, SMEs and universities. This is a template for a tech-led track with a European defence-industrial state.

CDF VADM Aaron Beng made the first-ever official visit to Lithuania on 7–8 April 2025. He met the Lithuanian CHOD and Defence Minister, toured an infantry battalion, saw a drone demonstration and was briefed on conscript intake. Lithuania signalled interest in defence-industry and cyber cooperation. This is the closest analogue for a first step with an eastern-flank NATO state.

Lithuania's CHOD Gen. Vaikšnoras made a reciprocal working visit to Singapore in February 2026. He called on the CDF, witnessed the launch of Exercise SG Ready (Total Defence) and spoke at GKS CSC's Distinguished Leaders Dialogue. RSN offshore patrol vessels are being built in Lithuania. These are concrete low-cost tools (PME dialogue and Total Defence exposure) that are transferable to Poland.

frame.question: What can the SAF learn from how Poland is building mass, counter-drone defence and national resilience at speed, and what is a realistic first step to engage a partner we barely know?
want: A clear picture of how Poland generates mass quickly: manpower, reserves, procurement and the money behind them.
Transferable lessons on counter-UAS and layered air defence, learned under live drone incursions.
Two or three low-cost entry points the SAF could open within 12 months.
Named Polish counterparts and venues where SAF officers can listen and be heard.
dont_want: A shopping list. Poland's equipment choices answer a different threat, terrain and budget.
Engagement framed as alignment against any third country. Keep it professional and method-focused.
Anything beyond open sources, or exchanges that need classified access to be useful.
Duplicating what the SAF already learns from close partners. Focus on what is distinctively Polish.

conops.text: About a month after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland adopted the Homeland Defence Act, which legally requires defence spending of at least 3% of GDP.
conops.headline: Homeland Defence Act sets a 3% floor

conops.text: Poland planned to spend the equivalent of 4% of GDP on defence in 2023, which would be the highest current level in NATO.
conops.headline: 4% of GDP budgeted for 2023

conops.text: NATO's June 2024 estimates put Poland at 4.12% of GDP for 2024, up from 3.92% in 2023, the highest share in the Alliance.
conops.headline: NATO's top spender as a share of GDP

conops.text: Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said Poland would boost defence spending to 5% of GDP.
conops.headline: 5% of GDP ambition announced

conops.text: The 2026 draft budget planned record defence spending equal to 4.8% of GDP, about $55bn, alongside a lower overall deficit.
conops.headline: Record 2026 defence budget: 4.8% of GDP

conops.text: NATO figures showed Poland putting 54.4% of its 2025 defence spending into equipment, the highest equipment share in the Alliance, out of a total of about $44.3bn.
conops.headline: Equipment-heavy rearmament

conops.text: The NATO Secretary General's Annual Report put Poland's 2025 defence spending at 4.3% of GDP, the highest in the Alliance and above the new 3.5% core benchmark.
conops.headline: NATO annual report: Poland highest at 4.3%

conops.text: NATO's 2026 estimates put Poland at 4.68% of GDP, already above the 3.5% core target, although Lithuania (5.33%), Estonia (5.11%) and Latvia (4.92%) are now estimated higher.
conops.headline: NATO 2026 estimate: about 4.7% of GDP

conops.text: Shift away from the post-Cold-War expeditionary posture back to territorial defence.
conops.headline: Back to territorial defence

conops.text: The 1st Legions Infantry Division is reactivated; it is to become the largest Polish formation, with Polish and South Korean equipment.
conops.headline: New division stands up

conops.text: Poland confirms the roughly €2B Eastern Shield belt along the Belarus and Kaliningrad borders: barriers, bunkers, sensors, electronic warfare and counter-drone systems.
conops.headline: Eastern Shield confirmed

conops.text: Russian drones cross into Polish airspace in a deliberate probe of air defences and public trust.
conops.headline: Drone incursion tests air defence

conops.text: Poland orders 18 SAN very-short-range counter-drone batteries from Kongsberg (about $1.6B), designed around lessons from Ukraine.
conops.headline: Counter-drone batteries ordered

conops.text: NATO and Ukraine open JATEC in Bydgoszcz, the first joint NATO–Ukraine body, to analyse and train on lessons from the war.
conops.headline: JATEC opens in Poland

relations.text: President Andrzej Duda called on NATO members to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP, using Poland's own spending level to press for a higher Alliance norm.
relations.headline: Duda presses allies to spend 3%

relations.text: NATO Review presented Poland, alongside Germany, as a country shifting the dial on European defence expenditure, which strengthens Warsaw's standing inside the Alliance.
relations.headline: NATO holds up Poland as a burden-sharing model

relations.text: At the Hague summit, Poland and the other Allies committed to spend 5% of GDP by 2035 (3.5% on core defence plus 1.5% on defence- and security-related spending); the Foreign Minister attended for Poland.
relations.headline: Hague summit: 5% by 2035

relations.text: Poland signs a second large K2 tank contract with South Korea, putting it on course for more tanks than the UK, Germany, France and Italy combined.
relations.headline: Second K2 deal with South Korea

relations.text: Poland's aim is to turn its buying spree into an arsenal for NATO: procurement from Polish firms has roughly quadrupled since 2022 to about $8.2B a year.
relations.headline: From buyer to arsenal

relations.text: South Korea's Army chief observes parts of exercise CZARNY OBROŃCA-26 and discusses wider military and industrial cooperation, the clearest sign yet of a non-European partner watching Polish exercises.
relations.headline: Korean Army chief watches a Polish exercise

budget.text: defence spending as a share of GDP has roughly doubled since 2022, from about 2.2-2.4% to about 4.5% in 2025 and about 4.7-4.8% in 2026, and real spending rose by about $17bn between 2022 and 2025. Growth is likely to level off near 5%, because Baltic allies now match or pass Poland's share and NATO's cash-basis accounting front-loads advance payments on multi-year orders.

personnel.text: Strength has grown from about 205,000 at the end of 2024 to more than 220,000 in 2026, toward a stated 300,000. Recruiting, training and keeping that many people is now the main limit, not money.

conops.text: the posture has moved from about 2% of GDP to a legislated, equipment-heavy rearmament (a 3% floor in law and the Alliance's highest equipment share in 2025). Poland is on track to stay well above NATO's 3.5% core target long before 2035, so the main question now is absorbing and crewing the new equipment rather than funding it. This judgement rests on the spending data; force-structure sources were not collected.

relations.text: Poland uses its top-spender status as leverage inside NATO, pressing allies for higher targets (3% in 2025) and backing the Hague 5% commitment, and NATO itself presents Poland as a burden-sharing model. Expect Warsaw to keep pushing Alliance spending norms upward. Bilateral supplier and treaty relationships were not verified in this pass.

relation.text: Poland's anchor ally and largest source of new heavy equipment: Abrams tanks, HIMARS-based launchers, Apache helicopters and F-35A fighters.
Second pillar of the rearmament: K2 tanks under the Wilk programme and FA-50 light combat aircraft, with local production and a widening military relationship.
Poland is NATO's top spender as a share of GDP and is held up by the Alliance as a burden-sharing model; it backed the pledge of 5% of GDP by 2035.
Main source of combat lessons: Poland hosts the NATO–Ukraine JATEC centre, and Ukrainian trainers coach Polish and allied troops on drone warfare.
Kongsberg supplies 18 SAN very-short-range counter-drone batteries, the core of Poland's new drone defence layer.
The Italian–Polish Defence & Dual Use Forum gives Polish commanders a recurring stage on land warfare after Ukraine.

institutions.name: Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW / Osrodek Studiow Wschodnich)
institutions.note: Poland's state-funded analytical centre on Russia, Eastern Europe, Germany and the Nordic-Baltic region. Its Security and Defence Department (Gotkowska) publishes rapid analyses of Russian pressure on Poland, such as the 10 Sep 2025 note on the drone incursion.

institutions.name: Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM)
institutions.note: State-funded foreign-policy institute. Its bulletins, Strategic Files and reports cover NATO deterrence, Polish nuclear-sharing options, Russian forces and the 2025 drone incursions (Lorenz, Kacprzyk, Terlikowski, Bryjka).

institutions.name: Casimir Pulaski Foundation (Fundacja im. Kazimierza Pulaskiego)
institutions.note: Independent, non-partisan security think tank that runs the Warsaw Security Forum. It published the 2024 RAND-supported wargame report on transforming the Polish Armed Forces. Russia declared it 'undesirable' in Dec 2025.

institutions.name: War Studies University (Akademia Sztuki Wojennej)
institutions.note: Poland's senior professional military education institution under the MoD. It hosts military-science publication repositories (sin.akademia.mil.pl, pbio.akademia.mil.pl) and is the natural counterpart for SAF PME and doctrine exchanges.

institutions.name: RAND Corporation - Poland research
institutions.note: US non-profit. Its 2025 report is the most complete English-language assessment of Polish modernisation, and it supported the Pulaski Foundation wargame. Much RAND work is US-government-sponsored.

institutions.name: International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS)
institutions.note: Publishes The Military Balance (reference data on Polish orders of battle and spending) and analyses of Polish naval expansion and Korean arms deals with Poland.

institutions.name: Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
institutions.note: US-based think tank with a steady stream of commentary on Polish modernisation. It ranges from bullish ('Poland Becomes a Defense Colossus') to critical, on unspent budgets, the Armed Forces Support Fund's off-budget bond financing and chaotic procurement.

institutions.name: Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)
institutions.note: Covers NATO budget data (Poland about 4.5% of GDP in 2025) and the case for permanent US basing in Poland, and hosts US-Poland defence-transformation and industrial-partnership events.

institutions.name: Rochan Consulting

institutions.name: Polityka Insight

items.text: Defence spending has roughly doubled since 2022 to about 4.5–4.8% of GDP, the highest share in NATO. The 2026 budget is a record ~200 billion złoty (~$55B).
items.headline: Rearming at record pace

items.text: Strength has grown from about 205,000 to more than 220,000 and is aimed at 300,000. Gen. Kukuła declared 2026 the 'year of reserves', with a reserve model of up to ~500,000.
items.headline: Building a mass army

items.text: Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace in September 2025. Poland is building the ~€2B Eastern Shield barrier and buying 18 counter-drone batteries, and its top general warns that Russia is building the capacity for war with NATO.
items.headline: A live threat on the border

items.text: Heavy equipment comes mainly from the US (Abrams, HIMARS, Apache, F-35) and South Korea (K2, FA-50). Buying from Polish firms has roughly quadrupled since 2022 to about $8.2B a year.
items.headline: Two suppliers and a growing home industry

items.text: Gen. Kukuła was reappointed Chief of the General Staff for three more years from October 2026. Maj Gen Ireneusz Nowak became Operational Commander in June 2026, and Bartosz Grodecki took over the President's National Security Bureau in May 2026.
items.headline: Steady at the top, new hands below

items.text: There is no defence agreement, staff talks or joint exercise. President Duda's June 2025 state visit, the first in over 20 years, touched on defence innovation, and Poland's deputy defence minister came to the Shangri-La Dialogue in 2025 and 2026.
items.headline: Ties with Singapore: thin but opening

talking_points.context: For a first conversation with a Polish defence counterpart, for example on the sidelines of the Shangri-La Dialogue or during a visit to Warsaw.

points.text: Congratulate Gen. Kukuła on his reappointment, and recognise Poland's lead in NATO defence spending.
points.why: Opens on current news and a point of national pride.

points.text: Acknowledge how fast Poland moved after the September 2025 drone incursion.
points.why: Shows we follow their situation closely, without taking a political line.

points.text: How do you train and hold reserves at the scale you are planning? What has the 'year of reserves' taught you so far?
points.why: Mobilisation is our biggest learning area and their current priority.

points.text: What does counter-drone defence cost you per kill across SAN, Narew and Wisła, and what would you do differently?
points.why: Draws out the lessons the SAF's new counter-UAS group needs.

points.text: How do JATEC's lessons from Ukraine reach your units, and could a partner outside NATO learn from them?
points.why: Tests whether a door is open to a non-NATO partner.

points.text: A peer conversation on National Service: Singapore's long experience of managing conscripts, reservists and Total Defence.
points.why: Our strongest offer on their top priority.

points.text: A low-cost first step: a counter-UAS expert exchange, or a Polish speaker at the Goh Keng Swee Command and Staff College.
points.why: Concrete, cheap and easy to say yes to.

points.text: Pitching or asking about equipment purchases. Keep it to methods, not materiel.
points.why: Their equipment answers a different threat, terrain and budget.

points.text: Framing cooperation as alignment against any third country.
points.why: Keeps the conversation professional and easy to defend.

points.text: Overstating today's ties. There is no defence agreement yet, so present this as a first step.
points.why: Credibility with a partner who knows how thin the ties are.
